briefs: For North Macedonia's A3 regulatory workstream, nbrm.mk is a single, dense, self-contained origin point: the bank publishes its own binding instruments in two parallel registers — supervision decisions (одлуки од областа на супервизијата) for banking and the ЗПУПС regulation set (including a dedicated index of the twelve payments bylaws) for payments — plus a layer of implementing упатства carrying the reporting deadlines, and statutory registers of banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions that reveal licensing decisions in effect. Legal force and exact entry-into-force dates trace to Службен весник на РСМ, whose full archive is subscription-gated, so the practical pipeline is NBRM consolidated PDFs plus Gazette citations, with the year-indexed Соопштенија stream as the fastest early-warning channel. The main structural weaknesses are the pre-adoption stage (no NBRM consultation hub was found; ENER is the likely but unconfirmed proxy) and the absence of any machine-readable feed, which forces HTML/PDF diffing. Collection must use a browser-grade fetcher — a plain fetch of an NBRM regulation index returned HTTP 403, which is a bot-defence hypothesis rather than evidence the page is dead.

For North Macedonia there is no ECB-style NBRM consultation portal: extensive Macedonian- and English-language searching surfaced only adopted decisions, consolidated texts and Council-session press releases on nbrm.mk, never a draft open for comment with a published deadline. The genuine consultation venue for banking and payments PRIMARY law is ENER (ener.gov.mk), the statutory national e-register where ministries must post draft laws with a Regulatory Impact Assessment (ПВР) and an open comment window — confirmed by live financial-sector items such as the draft amendments to the Law on Foreign Exchange Operations. For NBRM BYLAWS the earliest public signals are instead the annual Програма за работа and the 3-year Стратегиски план (forward-looking regulatory calendars), the NPAA EU-alignment matrices which date obligations by chapter and responsible institution, and industry channels (Македонска банкарска асоцијација) where NBRM consults banks non-publicly. Critically, the whole nbrm.mk host returns HTTP 403 to plain HTTP clients while remaining fully search-indexed, so this cell's core sources require a headless browser and should be treated as bot-defended-but-live, with national wire media and NBRM's social accounts as unblocked mirrors.

The English cross-border layer for North Macedonia banking and payments regulation is real and reasonably dense, anchored on three durable pillars: supranational assessments (European Commission enlargement reports, MONEYVAL, IMF Article IV, EBA CRR-equivalence opinion) and IFI reform documentation (World Bank payment-system and e-payments work, EBRD country strategies). Around these sits a fast-moving commercial layer of law-firm client alerts, mostly surfaced through Lexology, Mondaq and CEE Legal Matters and originating from a small set of regional firms (Karanovic & Partners, BDK, CMS, JPM) plus Skopje cooperating offices, which reliably restate effective and application dates. News monitoring is served by SeeNews, bne IntelliNews, Central Banking and MIA's English wire, with BIS's speech archive giving early English signals of NBRNM intentions. The main weaknesses are that no post-2008 FSAP could be evidenced, commercial regulatory-tracker vendor coverage of MK is unconfirmed, and this English layer lags badly on pre-adoption consultations, which stay in Macedonian on national portals.

North Macedonia's public-procurement intelligence for banking and payments is heavily centralised: ЕСЈН (e-nabavki.gov.mk), operated by the Биро за јавни набавки inside the Ministry of Finance, is the mandatory publication point for annual plans, notices, awards and realised contracts across every contracting authority, and it is the one source this cell cannot do without — though it is bot-defended (403 on plain fetch) and best reached through its .asmx service endpoints and dossier UUID URLs, with data.gov.mk and the skopjehacklab civic-tech scraper as machine-readable auxiliaries. The donor layer runs in parallel and is easier to collect: CFCD contracts all EU/IPA money, TED carries above-threshold and EU-funded MK notices with a clean API, and EBRD ECEPP plus World Bank project procurement plans (notably P176366 PFM, Ministry of Finance-implemented) pre-announce regulator and treasury modernisation 12-24 months ahead. Around these sit high-value enrichment sources — the Државна комисија за жалби по јавни набавки for award disputes and slipped timelines, the Државен завод за ревизија for what was actually delivered, and own-site document stores at Царинска управа, УЈП and ФЗО that publish full technical specifications as PDFs. The main open risks are the absence of a discoverable NBRSM procurement listing (forcing central-bank coverage through ESJN alone), an undefined CPV filter set, and no Albanian-language pass.

For North Macedonia the private-bank supplier ecosystem is genuinely the only public trace of compliance-driven buying: local-language tender searching confirmed that no aggregator carries private-sector bank RFPs, and the state e-Nabavki portal covers only public bodies. The productive layer is a small set of shared-infrastructure and regional vendors — CaSys (card processing for nearly every MK bank), KIBS (clearing, instant payments, SEPA readiness, OneID with Nextsense), ASEE/Asseco (ATMs, mergers, Basel/IFRS9 compliance work), Netcetera (3-D Secure/wallets for Halkbank) and Printec — plus MK trade press (bankarstvo.mk) that dates go-lives and mandates such as SCA from 1 March 2026 even when it does not name the supplier. The main blind spots are AML/sanctions-screening deals, which appear never to be announced publicly for MK, and tier-1 global core-banking vendors, for which no MK reference could be found at all; parent-group press rooms, job ads and conference agendas are the recommended next channels.

For North Macedonia, indirect regulatory-timing signals concentrate in three publicly reachable layers: (1) hiring — MK-language job boards (vrabotuvanje.com.mk, kariera.mk), the NBRSM careers page and the aggregator bankarstvo.mk, which republishes bank compliance/AML/regulatory-reporting ads and preserves them after the originals expire; (2) training and events — ABIT (the dedicated MK banking academy), the Economic Chamber's finance seminars, MASIT/KIBS payment-standard workshops, the FIU's statutory AML officer trainings, IORRM's annual CPD programme, and commercial conferences (Finelevate, MicroBalkans, the EACHA annual conference hosted in Skopje); (3) awards and certifications — Global Finance-type bank awards and licence milestones, surfaced first through the MK business-press cluster (Faktor, Makfax, Biznisvesti, MKD, MIA), which functions mainly as a pointer layer to primary organiser sites. English-language search is effectively blind for this cell — no MK bank vacancy surfaced in English — so Macedonian-language querying is load-bearing, while Albanian remains an uncovered language and LinkedIn remains legally off-limits to automated collection. Principal weaknesses to close next: enumerating licensed non-bank PSPs/EMIs from the NBRSM register, resolving the canonical domains of the conferences named only in press coverage, and starting daily snapshots of job listings so a hiring-surge baseline can ever be computed.

North Macedonia's enforcement-and-grievance layer for banking and payments is institutionally clear but unevenly published. The strongest, most structured source is the National Bank's annual 'Извештај за поплаките примени во банките и штедилниците' together with its Directorate for Consumer Protection and Financial Education (ЗПФЕ) — high-value but served from a bot-defended site that returned 403 to direct fetch. Independent corroboration comes from the Ombudsman's parliamentary annual reports, the State Audit Office (which does audit the National Bank itself), the Commission for Protection of Competition, the State Market Inspectorate, and the consumer NGO ОПМ, which usefully documents how complaints are routed between supervisors. The weak link is judicial output: the Constitutional Court publishes a genuinely enumerable decisions archive, but Administrative, Higher Administrative and Supreme Court judgments sit behind opaque legacy WebSphere portals with no full-text search, so browser-driven collection plus the Правдико legal portal as a tripwire is the realistic route to case-level signal.

For MK A3, the durable monitoring backbone is narrow but high quality: NBStat (nbstat.nbrm.mk) is a genuine PxWeb database with a standard API covering monetary, external and financial-accounts series, and ENER (ener.gov.mk) is the statutory consultation register that carries draft financial-sector laws and their comment deadlines before anything reaches the Official Gazette (slvesnik.com.mk), which remains the legally binding dating mechanism and offers a free-issue tier plus a queryable archived-issues index. The weak link is push notification and provenance: no RSS/e-mail alert endpoint could be confirmed anywhere on nbrm.mk, the site returns 403 to automated fetchers (bot-defended, not dead), data.gov.mk refused connection on the single attempt, and web.archive.org was unreachable from this agent — so archive depth for the regulator estate is asserted, never measured. Practical consequence: this cell should be operationalised as poll-plus-snapshot (crawl the NBRM supervision, reporting-obligation and register pages in browser context, hash every linked PDF, and push each new document to Wayback ourselves) rather than assuming existing archives already hold the version history. Two mechanical wins remain unclaimed and cheap: a feed-probe sweep (sitemap.xml, /feed, /wp-json) across the .gov.mk estate, and CDX indexing of commercial-bank tariff and general-conditions pages built off the NBRM bank register.

Primary banking/payments legislation in North Macedonia moves through a legible four-stage chain — ЕНЕР consultation, Влада session adoption ('утврден Предлог-закон'), Собрание committee and reading stages, then binding publication in Службен весник — and each stage has its own official publisher, so the cell is best covered by four monitors joined on bill title rather than one feed. The gazette is the only legally operative source and the only place transition articles fix compliance deadlines, but it exposes no feed or API and resisted automated fetching (TLS chain error), while sobranie.mk returned 403; both are treated here as bot-defended-but-live and need a browser-grade fetcher. Coverage cannot rest on ЕНЕР alone: civil-society monitoring indicates only about half of government bills reaching Parliament in 2023 were consulted there, making vlada.mk session readouts and Assembly agendas independent necessities rather than confirmations. Practical mirrors materially reduce risk — nbrm.mk and ufr.gov.mk host maintained consolidated statute texts with amendment gazette numbers in the filenames, mchamber.mk republishes draft and gazette PDFs, and AKADEMIKA offers licensed consolidation if a paid route is acceptable.

North Macedonia's non-central-bank compliance obligations for banking and payments are spread across six independent publishers, each with its own website and no common feed: УФР (AML/CFT rulebooks, suspicious-transaction indicators, typologies, supervision reports), АЗЛП (data-protection guidance for controllers), КХВ (capital-markets rulebooks), АСО (insurance by-laws and the only site observed to run its own public consultations), КЗК (merger/concentration clearances that flag bank ownership change), and УЈП (the fiscalisation stack that governs POS and fiscal-device vendors, with a clean type-filtered regulation register carrying effective dates). Two cross-cutting pointers make the cell tractable: ЕНЕР for pre-adoption drafts and consultation windows across all ministries, and Службен весник as the legally authoritative entry-into-force record from which deadlines are counted. Everything is Macedonian-language HTML/PDF with no RSS or API confirmed, so collection should be scheduled diff-crawling with mk keyword filters, plus a paid Gazette subscription and ASPI-routed FOI as fallbacks. Main open holes are the UJP approved-fiscal-device register and the KZK concentration-notification archive, both commercially high-value and both unresolved in this pass.

For North Macedonia, the EU side of the regulatory record is unusually rich and almost entirely English-language: the annual EC Country Report and the Cluster 3 screening report state chapter-by-chapter what remains to be transposed under Chapter 9 (financial services) and Chapter 4 (capital), while the Reform and Growth Facility Reform Agenda attaches money to dated reform steps. Sector-specific EU bodies add depth — EPC for SEPA scheme admission criteria and participant registers, EBA for the CRR/CRD equivalence gap analysis, and ECB Banking Supervision for the SSM–NBRM cooperation MoU. On the MK side the mandatory local-language sources are the NPAA (Национална програма за усвојување на правото на ЕУ) hosted by the Ministry of European Affairs and mirrored by line ministries, and the Sobranie's EU-flagged ('европско знаменце') bill pipeline with its conformity statements; twinning and TAIEX activity (CFCD, MoF, EU Delegation, partner central banks) is the best leading indicator of which directive gets transposed next. The main structural weakness is that no ready-made act-to-act transposition tracker exists — a deadline register has to be assembled by parsing NPAA tables and per-bill conformity statements.

For North Macedonia, the payments rule-setting layer is a three-body structure: NBRSM (owner/operator of the MIPS RTGS and overseer of everything else), KIBS AD Skopje (bank-owned clearing house running retail deferred-net clearing plus the domestic instant-payments platform, and an eIDAS trust service via OneID), and CaSys / Интернационален картичен систем (domestic card processing and card-system operation). The genuinely public, versioned rulebook is the NBRSM 'Правила за работа на МИПС'; KIBS exposes little more than a single operating-rules PDF and no visible tariff or admission-criteria page, and CaSys publishes almost nothing rule-shaped, so operator rules for retail clearing and cards must largely be inferred from NBRSM oversight documents, the National Payment System Council, banking-association bulletins and diffed bank general terms and conditions. The live deadline pressure in this cell is external: SEPA geographical accession (EPC approval March 2025, operational readiness from October 2025) and the Banca d'Italia-led TIPS Clone connection targeted for 2026, both of which will convert into participant-facing migration mandates. Practical constraint for collection: nbrm.mk returns 403 to naive fetchers, so the whole backbone of this cell needs browser-grade retrieval.

North Macedonia's supervised-entity register landscape is almost entirely centralised at the National Bank (НБРСМ/NBRNM), which under the 2022 Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems maintains statutory public registers for payment institutions, e-money institutions and payment system operators, alongside longstanding lists of licensed banks, savings houses, exchange offices (менувачници) and fast-money-transfer providers. All of these are HTML pages with occasional XLS/PDF attachments — no open-data API or archived history was found — and nbrm.mk answered a plain fetch with HTTP 403, so collection needs a browser-grade fetcher plus self-maintained snapshots for change detection. Secondary and cross-checking registers sit at the Central Registry (corporate identity), the Ministry of Finance (financial companies, unreachable this pass), the Deposit Insurance Fund (compulsory membership), the AML office UFR (obliged-entity taxonomies) and the Macedonian Banking Association (membership plus early sector notices). The main open items are the exact landing URL of the payment-institution register itself, whether agents/distributors are separately registered, and an Official Gazette route for dated licence grant/revocation events.

For North Macedonia, individual banks are a rich but fragmented source layer: there is no consolidated register of customer notices, so regulatory change must be observed bank-by-bank through Macedonian-language 'Соопштенија/Известувања' pages, tariff and General Terms PDFs carrying explicit effective dates, and the annual 'Извештај и податоци за Банката' (the local Pillar-3 disclosure). The single highest-leverage node is the MSE/SEI-NET disclosure stack, where every listed bank — Komercijalna, Stopanska, UNI, TTK, Centralna kooperativna, Silk Road and others — must file audited results, capital measures and assembly decisions, and where mse.mk offers a per-issuer RSS feed that makes filings machine-discoverable. Sparkasse is the cleanest template for the cell's target artefact, bundling the statutory fee report with dated tariff and General Terms amendments on a date-structured URL; Halkbank, CCB and Silk Road lack a confirmed notice index and will likely need document-diff monitoring instead. English-language material is effectively absent, and trade outlets bankarstvo.mk and pari.com.mk serve best as discovery pointers back to the banks' own primary documents.

The association layer in North Macedonia is unusually concentrated: the Македонска банкарска асоцијација (mba.mk) is the single banking trade body and covers all 13 banks, both savings houses, and the two payment-infrastructure members (KIBS clearing house, Macedonian Credit Bureau), while the Economic Chamber's Здружение на финансиски организации (mchamber.mk) is the cross-sector venue where banks, insurers, leasing and non-bank lenders consolidate comments before submitting them to the Ministry of Finance. Around these sit specialised bodies — АФД for non-bank/fintech lenders, МАСИТ for the ICT and payment-technology vendors, Асоцијација за е-трговија for the online-merchant side, and AmCham/FIC for foreign-investor advocacy in English. The dominant collection challenge is that positions are published as news items and loose PDFs rather than in an indexed consultations archive, and the chamber sites use unstable legacy ASPX/session URLs across two hosts. Two chamber homepages (north-western chamber, Union of Chambers) remain URL-unconfirmed and no Albanian-language search was performed, both of which should be closed before scheduled collection begins.

Macedonian-language business press for banking regulation clusters into three tiers: two wire-level agencies (Makfax, MIA) that render NBRM Council decisions, resolution-law implementing rules and SEPA/payment-system milestones fastest; a set of business portals and analytical outlets (Kapital and its Manager sub-site, Faktor, Ekonomija i biznis, Pari.com.mk, Biznis Info) that add market structure, rankings and expert reading of draft law; and one genuine sector specialist, Bankarstvo.mk, which is the highest signal-to-noise single feed for this cell. Time.mk is the key pointer layer — a single mk keyword sweep there identifies which outlet broke a story and exposes smaller portals, while Stopanska komora (mchamber.mk) acts as an upstream pointer because draft banking-law amendments circulate to members there before the press reports them. Two named cell outlets (Fokus, Sloboden Pecat) did not surface any banking-regulation articles in this run and are recorded as unverified rather than absent, and notably no MK press report of a specific supervisory sanction was retrieved — either a real reporting gap or a search-index blind spot that a dedicated enforcement pass should resolve. Albanian-language MK media and broadcast/interview formats are the two largest structural gaps left open by this cell's scope.
